title: Branches and Modulators Change the Ropes

scenes.tts: What happens when a rope grows stronger with voltage, or a modulator changes the ropes themselves?
scenes.visual: The voltage scale with its ropes. One rope begins to thicken; a dial labelled modulator appears beside the scale. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: What happens when a rope grows stronger with voltage, or a modulator changes the ropes themselves?

scenes.tts: A real neuron is not one compact patch. Each patch of dendrite has its own ropes, and passes current to its neighbours.
scenes.visual: A branching dendritic tree divided into small patches; each patch has a small voltage scale, and arrows of current flow between neighbouring patches.
scenes.narration: A real neuron is not one compact patch. Each patch of dendrite has its own ropes, and passes current to its neighbours.

scenes.tts: So the patches set each other's voltages. The length constant and the capacitance shrink and smooth what reaches the soma.
scenes.visual: Bumps from each site travel to the soma, arriving smaller and broader.
scenes.narration: So the patches set each other's voltages. The length constant and the capacitance shrink and smooth what reaches the soma.

scenes.tts: Polsky, Mel and Schiller stimulated two sites on thin dendrites of rat neocortical pyramidal neurons. First each alone, then both together.
scenes.visual: Scientist card: Polsky, Mel & Schiller, Nature Neuroscience (2004). Two stimulating electrodes on a thin branch, imaged by confocal microscopy.
scenes.narration: Polsky, Mel and Schiller stimulated two sites on thin dendrites of rat neocortical pyramidal neurons. First each alone, then both together.

scenes.tts: Picture their comparison as a graph. Along the bottom, the response expected if the two inputs simply added.
scenes.visual: Empty axes. X axis: expected response (sum of the two separate responses).
scenes.narration: Picture their comparison as a graph. Along the bottom, the response expected if the two inputs simply added.

scenes.tts: Up the side, the response actually measured. A point on the 45 degree line means linear addition.
scenes.visual: Y axis: measured response (both together). A dashed 45-degree line labelled linear.
scenes.narration: Up the side, the response actually measured. A point on the 45 degree line means linear addition.

scenes.tts: Inputs far apart, or on different branches, fell on the line. They summed linearly.
scenes.visual: Points in grey labelled 'different branches or far apart' fall along the dashed line.
scenes.narration: Inputs far apart, or on different branches, fell on the line. They summed linearly.

scenes.tts: Nearby inputs on one thin branch summed sigmoidally. The response rose slowly, then steeply, then levelled off.
scenes.visual: Points in orange labelled 'same thin branch, nearby' trace an S-shaped curve: slow, then steep, then flat.
scenes.narration: Nearby inputs on one thin branch summed sigmoidally. The response rose slowly, then steeply, then levelled off.

scenes.tts: So location set the combination rule. The result supports the idea that thin branches act as separate integrating subunits.
scenes.visual: The dendritic tree with each thin branch outlined as its own small unit.
scenes.narration: So location set the combination rule. The result supports the idea that thin branches act as separate integrating subunits.

scenes.tts: The steep phase is generally attributed to local regenerative events. NMDA receptors are thought to take part.
scenes.visual: The steep part of the S-curve is highlighted. A small NMDA receptor icon with the label 'thought to take part'.
scenes.narration: The steep phase is generally attributed to local regenerative events. NMDA receptors are thought to take part.

scenes.tts: Once glutamate and a co-agonist have bound, an NMDA receptor is a rope that thickens as the marker rises. Depolarization pushes out the magnesium ion that blocks it.
scenes.visual: On the voltage scale, a purple NMDA rope with glutamate and co-agonist drawn bound to the receptor; as the marker moves right it thickens and a small ion labelled Mg²⁺ pops out of the channel.
scenes.narration: Once glutamate and a co-agonist have bound, an NMDA receptor is a rope that thickens as the marker rises. Depolarization pushes out the magnesium ion that blocks it.

scenes.tts: Over the right voltage range, it thickens faster than its driving force shrinks. Then its pull grows.
scenes.visual: The NMDA rope's driving-force arrow shortens while the rope keeps thickening; over a marked voltage range its pull still grows.
scenes.narration: Over the right voltage range, it thickens faster than its driving force shrinks. Then its pull grows.

scenes.tts: Now modulators. A fast synapse adds a rope briefly. A modulator can instead change the ropes the cell already has.
scenes.visual: A brief red rope flashes on and off. Then the modulator dial turns and the standing ropes change thickness.
scenes.narration: Now modulators. A fast synapse adds a rope briefly. A modulator can instead change the ropes the cell already has.

scenes.tts: In sympathetic neurons, G q coupled, M one muscarinic receptors close KCNQ potassium channels. These carry the M current.
scenes.caption: In sympathetic neurons, Gq-coupled M1 muscarinic receptors close KCNQ potassium channels. These carry the M-current.
scenes.visual: A purple potassium rope tied near E_K, labelled KCNQ (M-current). Acetylcholine binds an M1 muscarinic receptor (Gq-coupled) beside it.
scenes.narration: In sympathetic neurons, Gq-coupled M1 muscarinic receptors close KCNQ potassium channels. These carry the M-current.

scenes.tts: In cells expressing these channels, depleting the membrane lipid pip two alone was enough to suppress the current. So the lipid itself can regulate the channel.
scenes.caption: In cells expressing these channels, depleting the membrane lipid PIP2 alone was enough to suppress the current. So the lipid itself can regulate the channel.
scenes.visual: Scientist card: Suh, Inoue, Meyer & Hille, Science (2006). PIP2 molecules removed from the membrane; the KCNQ current trace falls.
scenes.narration: In cells expressing these channels, depleting the membrane lipid PIP2 alone was enough to suppress the current. So the lipid itself can regulate the channel.

scenes.tts: Closing these channels removes a potassium rope. What happens to the response to the same current step?
scenes.visual: The KCNQ rope fades from the scale. An electrode icon injects a current step. On screen: Pause. What happens to the response to the same current step?
scenes.narration: Closing these channels removes a potassium rope. What happens to the response to the same current step?

scenes.tts: In a passive approximation, closing a potassium conductance raises the resting voltage a little and shrinks the bottom line. The same sustained current step then gives a larger steady change, and takes longer to reach the same fraction of it.
scenes.visual: The marker shifts slightly right. Two current-step responses, each measured from its own resting baseline: the KCNQ-closed response and a ghost KCNQ-open response start with the same initial slope; the KCNQ-closed response climbs to a larger steady amplitude, and 63% markers show it reaching that fraction later (longer time constant). Label: fixed-conductance passive approximation. Small print: a synaptic EPSP need not grow, since the cell has less driving force for excitation.
scenes.narration: In a passive approximation, closing a potassium conductance raises the resting voltage a little and shrinks the bottom line. The same sustained current step then gives a larger steady change, and takes longer to reach the same fraction of it.

scenes.tts: Closing them increases excitability. The neuron fires more to the same input.
scenes.visual: A current step gives more spikes after the muscarinic agonist than before.
scenes.narration: Closing them increases excitability. The neuron fires more to the same input.

scenes.tts: Dopamine on D one receptors is the harder case. In mouse striatal neurons, firing to the same injected current rose.
scenes.caption: Dopamine on D1 receptors is the harder case. In mouse striatal neurons, firing to the same injected current rose.
scenes.visual: Scientist card: Lahiri & Bevan, Neuron (2020). A matched current step: a spike raster before and after dopamine-axon stimulation, with more spikes after.
scenes.narration: Dopamine on D1 receptors is the harder case. In mouse striatal neurons, firing to the same injected current rose.

scenes.tts: It rose within hundreds of milliseconds. After one bout of stimulation, it stayed raised for at least ten minutes.
scenes.caption: It rose within hundreds of milliseconds. After one bout of stimulation, it stayed raised for at least 10 minutes.
scenes.visual: A timeline: firing rises within hundreds of milliseconds and stays raised past the 10-minute mark.
scenes.narration: It rose within hundreds of milliseconds. After one bout of stimulation, it stayed raised for at least 10 minutes.

scenes.tts: With synaptic receptors blocked and drift controlled, the cell's own conductances or active currents must have changed. A spike count cannot say which channel.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale with a question mark over which rope changed. Label: same current, more spikes. Note on screen: receptor blockers; matched current-only control trials.
scenes.narration: With synaptic receptors blocked and drift controlled, the cell's own conductances or active currents must have changed. A spike count cannot say which channel.

scenes.tts: Branches can make a rope grow with voltage. Modulators change the ropes themselves. The rule tells you what kind of change to look for.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: NMDA ropes can grow with voltage; modulators change the ropes the cell has. The rule tells you what kind of change to look for.
scenes.narration: Branches can make a rope grow with voltage. Modulators change the ropes themselves. The rule tells you what kind of change to look for.
